Photograph: U.S. Southern Command View image in fullscreen On 23 August, the US Southern Command executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the eastern Pacific. Photograph: U.S. Southern Command Americas US strikes a vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing 2 people in first attack in months US Southern Command has struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing two accused of trafficking drugs Maya Yang and agencies Mon 24 Aug 2026 17.40 EDT First published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 16.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US military has launched a deadly strike on a vessel in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of drug trafficking. On Monday, US Southern Command (SouthCom) announced it “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific”. “Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed two narco-terrorists,” SouthCom added. Southern Command did not provide evidence for the vessel’s alleged involvement in drug trafficking. In a statement on the strikes, Francis L Donovan, SouthCom’s commander general, said: “We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists – disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership and eliminating cartel terror across the region.” “This operation is a powerful demonstration of our lethal precision, overwhelming capability, and absolute resolve to protect the US homeland,” Donovan added. A pixelated black-and-white video posted to SouthCom’s X account on Monday showed a vessel moving through the water before it was struck by an explosion that produced a large flash of light. Monday’s strike marks the latest in a series of US military strikes since the Donald Trump administration launched what it described as a campaign targeting “narco-terrorists” smuggling drugs into the US, despite numerous reports indicating that the strikes have done little to stem the flow of drugs into the country. It brings the overall death toll to 223 people killed in 67 strikes during the nearly year-long US campaign of bombing alleged drug boats off Latin America’s Caribbean coast and in the eastern Pacific Ocean. US Southern Command says the campaign has resulted in the destruction of 64 speedboats, three “low-profile” ships and a semisubmersible craft. The latest strike comes as the Trump administration pursues deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the US to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal. Ecuador launched similar missions with the US in March. The Trump administration’s boat bombing campaign began in early September and has left numerous survivors, but most of them have never been recovered. US Southern Command said in a separate statement on Monday that there have been more than 20 search and rescue efforts overall, almost all of which were unsuccessful. According to data compiled from the command’s social media posts, the strikes have generated 28 survivors with only three people ever being rescued – one person during a strike in March who was transferred to the Costa Rican Coast Guard, and two wounded people who were later repatriated to their home countries of Ecuador and Colombia . The very first strike in September 2025 left two survivors who were killed in a second, follow-up strike. When that became public, it drew concern from some lawmakers and those who study military law. The White House insisted it was done “in self-defense” to ensure the boat was destroyed and in accordance with armed conflict laws. Despite the defense department framing the strikes as attacks against “narco-terrorism”, it has provided little evidence on whether the vessels were actually transporting drugs. The attacks have been condemned as extrajudicial killings by the United Nations and other humanitarian organizations. According to a 2020 report by the US Drug Enforcement Administration, 74% of the cocaine reaching the US arrived through the Pacific while only 8% came from fast boats from the Caribbean. Critics have questioned the overall legality of the boat strikes as well as their effectiveness, in part because the fentanyl behind many fatal overdoses is typically trafficked to the US over land from Mexico, where it is produced with chemicals imported from China and India. The Pentagon’s watchdog said in May that it plans to look into whether the US military followed an established targeting framework when carrying out the strikes. However, the evaluation is focused specifically on what’s known as the six-phase Joint Targeting Cycle and not on the legality of the strikes, the inspector general’s office said. Meanwhile, an investigation by the Latin American Center for Investigative Journalism (Clip) this year identified 13 previously unidentified victims of US vessel attacks. All came from impoverished communities across Latin America and the Caribbean and several were fishers with no indication of involvement in the drug trade, it found. “There are communities where they stopped fishing for several weeks – and if they do that, people go hungry – because they were terrified of being bombed,” María Teresa Ronderos, Clip director, said at the time of the report’s release. Other families continue to grieve as they seek answers about their relatives killed in US airstrikes. “If the boat was carrying so much cocaine and then exploded and caught fire, where is the evidence? Where is the cocaine? That is what I want to know. I know Ricky. He was a fisherman. That was his life,” Titus, the brother of Ricky Joseph, one of the 13 people identified in the CLIP investigation, said in June from the Carribean island of St Lucia. Bonny Reichert/Supplied In January of 1948, Saul Reichert landed at Pier 21 in Halifax, alone in the world. He was 17, with one English pound and a few U.S. dollars in his pocket. He was a survivor of Auschwitz and had lost his mother and five sisters in the Holocaust. There was no question of returning to his hometown in Poland. Mr. Reichert was a participant in the War Orphans Project, the product of an agreement between the Canadian Jewish Congress and the Canadian government that ultimately saw 1,123 Jewish survivors under the age of 18 immigrate to Canada. It was also the first crack in the notorious Canadian immigration policy that had shut out Jews fleeing the Nazis before and during the Second World War. Most of the orphans were sponsored by Jewish families in Montreal and Toronto, but Saul was one of 28 headed for Alberta, travelling across the country to Edmonton, where he was welcomed by a sponsoring family. Within two years, he owned a lunch counter and spoke English, launching a successful business career in restaurants and real estate and becoming an active member of Edmonton’s Jewish community, showing a remarkable resilience and positive attitude that continued throughout his life. “He didn’t look back, he looked forward and lived in the present,” said David Margolus, an Edmonton lawyer whose parents sponsored young Saul on his arrival in the city in 1948. Mr. Margolus was born two years later and Mr. Reichert became a presence in his life that continued until Mr. Reichert’s death. “He was in every sense a part of our family. He was like an older brother to me.” Mr. Reichert, who died in Toronto on July 24 at 95, never stopped being thankful for his chance at a new life. “To come to a country like Canada was really the difference between day and night,” he recalled in a 1985 video testimony produced for the Jewish Archives and Historical Society of Edmonton and Northern Alberta. Open this photo in gallery: Saul Reichert at age 17 in Pegnitz, Germany, in 1947. Photo courtesy of the Reichert family “He was a very optimistic person, stubbornly optimistic,” said Bonny Reichert, a Toronto food writer and the youngest of Mr. Reichert’s four daughters, who chronicled her father’s life in her own memoir, How to Share an Egg, published in 2025. “He didn’t expect to survive and when he did, he saw it as a marvellous second chance.” “Seeing things in a positive way and thinking things would get better soon, that was Saul to a T,” said his eldest daughter, Rochelle, who recalled that her father didn’t dwell on what he lived through as a child and teenager. “He didn’t want to burden his children and didn’t want us to experience what he had,” she said. Shlomo Reichert was born on Dec. 17, 1930, in Pabianice, a small city adjacent to Lodz in central Poland, the only son of Betzalel Reichert and his wife, the former Udel Rotblat, who also had four daughters together. A fifth girl, Saul’s half-sister, was the daughter of Betzalel’s first wife, who had died. The family owned a paint-supply shop and lived a middle-class life, though they were affected by the Depression. In the video, Mr. Reichert recounts that he had a wonderful childhood, surrounded by a warm and loving family. That childhood ended in 1939, with the death of his father from natural causes and the Nazi invasion of Poland. He was 8. In 1940, the family was forced into Pabianice’s Jewish ghetto, where he was nevertheless able to continue some schooling. Two years later, they were forcibly sent to the ghetto in Lodz where conditions were much more difficult. There was no school and hardly any food. “People were sitting in the streets waiting to die and nobody could help them,” he recalled. Then Saul managed to get work as a sorter in a church where the authorities had sent pillows, duvets and other bedding taken from Jewish families. Workers like Saul would slash them open, and then separate the feathers and down, which were ultimately shipped off to Germany. Reacting to Saul’s inherent charm, a supervisor named Mr. Sharp took a liking to the boy and found a job for Saul’s mother distributing food, giving the family better access to scarce rations. “All of a sudden, our fate in the ghetto became better,” Saul said. There was another advantage to the sorting job. Desperate Jews would occasionally hide jewellery or cash which would emerge when the bedding was ripped open and could be traded for something of immediate value. “For a diamond ring, you’d be lucky if you got two or three loaves of bread,” Saul said. In the fall of 1944, the Lodz ghetto was emptied. Saul and his family were loaded into rail cars and sent to Auschwitz-Birkenau. Arriving at the camp, they were surrounded by armed German guards screaming at them, accompanied by dogs. “All of a sudden, they separated the women and the men.” It was the last time Saul saw his mother and sisters. “You could see the crematorium in the background,” Mr. Reichert recalled in 1985. “The people who looked sick and were very thin went to the other side and were never seen again.” But Saul, despite his small stature, was nevertheless selected for forced labour and ended up in a sub-work camp called Gleiwitz, where he hauled railway ties. Open this photo in gallery: Mr. Reichert, pictured in 1947, leaves his daughters, Rochelle, Jerell, Adell and Bonny, as well as 10 grandchildren and 10 great-grandchildren. Photo courtesy of the Reichert family As the Red Army advanced in early 1945, the Nazis sent the remaining concentration camp inmates north on the infamous death marches. Saul and a cousin ended up on a train that took them to Germany, where they were liberated by U.S. soldiers in May of 1945. Hiding in a barn, he was initially skeptical but when he heard the troops speaking English, he was elated. “I was so excited. I’m going to live. I’m not going to die,” he recalled later. Saul survived over the next two years working in a kitchen for American troops and made a brief foray into cigarette smuggling. Then he and his cousin heard about the opportunity to get a visa. He told officials he wanted to go to New York, not knowing he would be heading for Canada. His cousin, who was already 18, was excluded from the Canadian program. When he arrived in Edmonton, the Margolus family helped Mr. Reichert get started, finding him a job at Teddy’s Lunch, a deli and grocery store known for its corned beef sandwiches and chili con carne. Working seven days a week, he ended up buying the business two years later with help from the Margolus family. He soon paid off the loan. Mr. Reichert bought a couple of other luncheonettes and opened the Carousel, a 250-seat dining room and bar. He expanded Teddy’s and with partners bought stakes in other restaurants and a hotel. As Edmonton grew, Mr. Reichert bought farmland in nearby Beaumont and became a house builder and developer. A street in the town bears his name. Mr. Reichert married in 1956 and with his wife, Toby, had four girls. As teens, the sisters ended up working the cash or acting as a hostess or server at one of the restaurants. Saul and Toby were keen card players, particularly bridge, and Saul enjoyed poker as well. When they became more prosperous, they began to winter in Arizona but still felt most at home in Edmonton. After retiring, they eventually moved to Toronto, to be closer to their daughters. Mrs. Reichert died in 2021. In 2004, the Reicherts endowed the Toby and Saul Reichert Holocaust Lecture at the University of Alberta’s Wirth Institute for Austrian and Central European Studies. The series features an annual lecture at the university by a prominent scholar of the Holocaust. Though he didn’t harp on it, Mr. Reichert did have his views on the causes of the Holocaust. He lay the blame firmly at the feet of the German people. “Look at the newsreels of 1933 to 1944. They were cheering him [Hitler] on,” Mr. Reichert said in his video testimonial, blaming the German people for failing to rebel against the Nazi regime. “There must never be a nation who can do what the Germans did and get away with it,” he said in the video. Mr. Reichert leaves his daughters, Rochelle, Jerell, Adell and Bonny, as well as 10 grandchildren and 10 great-grandchildren. You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here .
